figures.caption: Fig. 6. Electrochemical performance of high-entropy LM0.2PS at 25 ◦C. a, Potential response of Li|LM0.2PS|Li symmetric cells undergoing a CCD measurement at 25 ◦C. b, Long-term galvanostatic cycling of the Li|LM0.2PS|Li symmetric cell at 0.5 mA cm−2. The inset shows selected Nyquist plots collected after representative cycling stages, illustrating the evolution of the interfacial impedance response. converted into the instantaneous galvanostatic polarization voltage, the overall evolution of the interfacial response suggests an initial interfacial rearrangement followed by a relatively stable impedance behavior at extended cycling times. Taken together, these results show that LM0.2PS not only exhibits a higher CCD, but also enables a more durable Li-metal interface than pristine LGPS, thereby improving tolerance against long- term Li plating/stripping. Supplementary Fig. 3b depicts the linear relationship between the applied voltage and the steady-state current of LM0.2PS. figures.label: S9
figures.caption: Supplementary Fig.9. Micro-morphology and elemental analysis of the LM0.2PS electrolyte. a, SEM image of the synthesized LM0.2PS powder. b, Corresponding element mappings of LM0.2PS, indicating homogeneous dispersion of all constituent elements within the particle. Elemental mapping images based on EDS analysis demonstrate the homogeneous distribution of the high-entropy dopants (Si, Ge, Sn, Ti, W) throughout the particle, without observable phase segregation or local enrichment. Furthermore, the P and S maps show consistent spatial overlap, supporting the structural integrity of the PS43- tetrahedral framework. These results confirm the successful incorporation of multiple cations into the LGPS-type lattice, forming a chemically uniform high-entropy LM0.2PS solid-state electrolyte.
